part_title: Account Onboarding, Billing, Tagging and Organization Policy Governance

scenes.title: Created, invited and moved accounts have different setup steps
scenes.visual_overview: The three panels compare a new account created by AWS Organizations, an existing invited account, and an account moved between organizations.
visual_walkthrough: Created member account may receive OrganizationAccountAccessRole for management-account administration
Invited existing account does not automatically receive the same role; review access, logging, controls and costs
Moving between organizations requires removal from the old one and acceptance into the new one, with billing and policies rechecked
scenes.visual_example: An account invited from an existing AWS environment needs a deliberate access and baseline review; it should not be treated identically to a new Account Factory-created account.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Organization membership doesn't automatically configure every administrator role, service integration or governance baseline.
scenes.narration: This slide compares three account onboarding situations in AWS Organizations. The three columns are alternatives, not a single sequence. First, when the management account creates a new member account, Organizations normally creates the OrganizationAccountAccessRole, enabling authorized management-account principals to assume it. The trust relationship and IAM permissions still govern access. In the middle, an existing account is invited into the organization. That invitation does not automatically install the same administration role. Follow the review icons beneath it: check existing administrator access, security logging and policies, and financial responsibilities before declaring the account onboarded. On the right, moving an account between two organizations requires satisfying removal prerequisites, leaving or being removed from the original organization, and joining the destination through an accepted invitation. After the move, re-evaluate effective SCPs, governance integrations and billing. This is different from moving between organizational units within one organization. The key takeaway is that account membership and account readiness are different things. Use the correct onboarding path, verify the baseline and avoid assuming an invitation reproduces every capability of a newly created account.

scenes.title: Organizations: billing benefits and governance features
scenes.visual_overview: The slide distinguishes consolidated billing, organization all-features governance, eligible commitment discount sharing and independent IAM boundaries.
visual_walkthrough: Consolidated billing brings eligible member usage and payment together while all-features mode enables additional governance
Management-account billing settings determine sharing of eligible Reserved Instance and Savings Plans benefits
Shared billing benefits do not grant IAM resource access or transfer ownership; resource quotas and reservation capacity are separate
scenes.visual_example: Two accounts may share an eligible Savings Plans discount through organization settings without either account gaining permission to start or delete resources in the other.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Centralized billing is a financial relationship; governance and authorization require distinct policies and operations.
scenes.narration: This visual explains what AWS Organizations changes financially, and what it does not change about security. Begin on the left. Consolidated billing groups eligible usage and charges from member accounts under a payer relationship. Organizations all-features mode adds supported governance capabilities, and enabling it can involve approval from invited accounts. It is not a reversible switch back to billing-only. Now move to the upper-right panel. The management account controls eligible discount sharing for Reserved Instances and Savings Plans according to current AWS billing rules and configured sharing settings. Follow the colored arrows to participating accounts: multiple accounts may benefit financially without transferring resource ownership. The lower-right panel is the security boundary. A shared discount does not give a user IAM access to another account's EC2 instances, S3 buckets or other resources. Nor does it automatically transfer quotas or capacity-reservation rights. For architectural decisions, separate three questions: who pays, which savings can be shared, and who is authorized to use a resource. Organizations can improve financial efficiency while preserving the account boundaries required for security and operational accountability.

scenes.title: Tag policies standardize; creation controls require presence
scenes.visual_overview: Three panels distinguish standardizing key/value taxonomy, enforcing mandatory tag presence at creation, and securing tags for cost allocation and ABAC.
visual_walkthrough: Organizations tag policies define supported tag keys, capitalization and allowed values, with enforcement where supported
IAM, SCP and service request-tag conditions or provisioning controls can require critical tags when the resource is created
Cost allocation and ABAC require trustworthy tags and restrictions on later tag mutations, including testing untagged resources
scenes.visual_example: A tag policy standardizing CostCenter capitalization does not guarantee every new EC2 resource includes CostCenter; a separate applicable request-tag condition is needed where supported.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Taxonomy compliance, mandatory tag presence and authorization to change security-sensitive tags are distinct controls.
scenes.narration: This slide teaches a common governance distinction: a tag policy that standardizes tag names does not necessarily require every resource to have those tags. Start with the left panel. AWS Organizations tag policies can define supported keys, capitalization and allowed values, and can check or enforce specified tagging operations where supported. The three arrows illustrate those taxonomy choices. Move to the upper-right panel. When a business requires a CostCenter or Project tag on creation, use appropriate service, IAM or SCP request-tag conditions and supported provisioning controls. The actual create API must support the selected condition keys, so test untagged requests rather than assuming blanket enforcement. In the lower-right panel, the focus changes from creation to use. Cost-allocation reports depend on meaningful tags, and attribute-based access control can use tags for authorization. If an unauthorized principal can add or rewrite a security-sensitive tag, a well-written ABAC policy may still be undermined. Restrict tag modification and test service exceptions. The closing principle is that standardized key names, required tag presence and protected tag lifecycle are related, but they solve three separate governance problems.

scenes.title: Organization policies: data-use preferences and backup plans
scenes.visual_overview: A two-part policy comparison covers organization-scoped AI data-use preferences and inherited AWS Backup plan intent, followed by operational execution verification.
visual_walkthrough: AI services opt-out policies apply supported data-use preferences to relevant service and organization scopes, requiring current service-specific review
Organizations backup policies express supported schedules, windows, selection and copy requirements inherited by affected accounts
Backup-job evidence, permissions, resource eligibility and restore testing verify that intended backups occurred; a policy alone proves nothing
scenes.visual_example: A centralized backup policy might specify daily backups and cross-account copies, yet missing role permissions or unsupported resource selection can still cause jobs to fail.
scenes.visual_synthesis: Organization policies express intent; service configurations, job outcomes and restore evidence demonstrate that the desired control actually worked.
scenes.narration: This final section compares two organization policy families that represent centrally managed intent. On the left, AI services opt-out policies help govern supported service data-use preferences within configured organization scopes. The important caution on the slide is that supported services and data-use terms differ; do not assume one policy overrides every possible AI product's terms. On the upper right, AWS Organizations backup policies define supported backup-plan behavior such as schedules, backup windows, resource selections and copy requirements for member accounts. The icons show that central policy can guide consistent recovery-point operations. But follow the lower-right proof-of-execution sequence. The existence of a policy does not mean a resource was eligible, the backup role had permission, a job completed or a restore would work. Teams must inspect effective plans and resource coverage, monitor backup-job results and perform meaningful recovery tests. Local workload owners still have operational responsibility for successful recovery. The architectural lesson is to distinguish governance intent from observed compliance: policies define what should happen, while service evidence proves what actually happened.
